mainTopic: Damage from a broken כד and objects in רשות הרבים: בור's exemptions, הפקר, and liability for אונס
overview: The amud opens with רב's ruling about a כד that broke in רשות הרבים. The owner pays for the clothes of someone who slips, but not for the person's injury, because the ground hurt him. שמואל holds the reverse. Objects left in the street are learned from בור, and בור is exempt for vessels, so the owner pays for the person but not for the clothes. רב answers that only an object made הפקר is like a בור. רב אושעיא then brings a ברייתא that seems to trouble both of them. The גמרא shows that each can explain it his own way: רב by limiting it to הפקר objects, and שמואל by tying the flask case to רבי יהודה. רבי אלעזר's two versions about a flask breaking on a stone are linked to רבי נתן's rule. Finally the גמרא asks what רבי יהודה in the משנה means by 'with intent.' רבה's answer leads to a challenge that the תורה exempts an אנוס. The ברייתא brought to answer that challenge continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רב: No payment for the person's own injury, because the ground hurt him
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that the owner of the broken כד is exempt for the bodily injury of the one who slipped, since the ground caused the injury.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for the person himself, the owner is exempt, because it was the ground that injured him.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the end of רב's ruling, reported by רב יהודה. The owner of the broken כד pays for the victim's clothes, but not for the victim's own body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person was not hurt by the jug or by the water. He was hurt when he hit the ground. Nobody owns the ground, so nobody is responsible for that blow, and the owner of the כד is exempt for the bodily injury.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt; does not have to pay
The ordinary ground that nobody owns

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two halves of רב's ruling. He says the owner is liable for the clothes and exempt for the person. שמואל will say exactly the reverse.

phrases.english: But [for] the person himself — [the owner is] exempt;
the ground of the world injured him.
phrases.notes: Literally 'the ground of the world': the ordinary ground everyone walks on, which belongs to nobody.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל הוּא עַצְמוֹ – פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רב's ruling, which began just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner of a broken כד is exempt for the bodily injury of someone who slips on it, because the ground caused the injury (and by implication he is liable for the clothes).

steps.title: שמואל: Stone, knife and load are learned from the pit, so the pit's exemptions apply
steps.stepSummary: שמואל argues that damage from objects left in the street is learned from בור, so the exemptions of בור (people and vessels) carry over to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: When I told this to שמואל, he said to me: after all, we learned the laws of someone's stone, knife and load from the laws of his pit. So for all of them I read the פסוק this way: 'ox', and not a person; 'donkey', and not vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה reports that שמואל disagreed with רב. שמואל begins by laying down the source he will use against רב's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Objects left lying in the street are treated like a בור. The פסוק about בור mentions an ox and a donkey, and the חכמים read this as 'not a person' and 'not vessels.' Since a broken כד works like a בור, those same exemptions should apply to it, and that already seems to clash with רב making the owner pay for the clothes.

keyTerms.meaning: After all; since it is already known that...
Pit; one of the main categories of damage
Vessels and other belongings, including clothes

phrases.english: When I said it before Shmuel,
phrases.notes: 'I' is רב יהודה, who passed on רב's ruling.

phrases.english: he said to me:
After all, his stone, his knife, and his load —
we learned [them] from his pit,
and regarding all of them I read:
"ox" — and not a person,
"donkey" — and not vessels.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אַמְרִיתַהּ קַמֵּיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל, אָמַר לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: שמואל challenges רב's ruling from the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that the owner of the כד is liable for the clothes but exempt for the person
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Objects in the street are learned from בור, and בור is exempt for vessels. So the owner should not pay for the clothes.

steps.title: שמואל: The person exemption is only for death, so the result is the reverse of רב
steps.stepSummary: שמואל limits 'not a person' to a case where the person died. For an injury, the owner is liable for a person and exempt for vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this applies to a case of death. But for injuries, he is liable for a person and exempt for vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל finishes his argument by narrowing the 'not a person' exemption. The result is the exact opposite of רב's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Not a person' means only that a בור owner does not pay when a person is killed. When a person is merely injured, he does pay. The exemption for vessels has no such limit, so for the broken כד שמואל holds: pay for the injured person, do not pay for the clothes.
steps.whatToRemember: רב says the owner pays for the clothes but not for the person. שמואל says he pays for the person but not for the clothes.

phrases.english: And these words apply regarding death,
phrases.notes: 'These words' are 'not a person' from the line before.

phrases.english: but regarding injuries —
[for] a person he is liable,
and [for] vessels he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי לְעִנְיַן קְטָלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes שמואל's argument by limiting the 'not a person' exemption to death.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to שמואל, the owner of the broken כד pays for the bodily injury but not for the damaged clothes.

steps.title: רב's answer: The pit comparison applies only to ownerless objects
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that for רב, objects are learned from בור only when the owner made them הפקר. Otherwise they count as his property, and he pays even for vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how would רב answer? This comparison applies when he made them ownerless. But when he did not make them ownerless, it is his property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how רב would answer שמואל, and gives רב's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב agrees that a stone, knife or load is learned from בור, but only once the owner has given up ownership of it. If he still owns the object, it is simply his property causing damage. In that case the בור exemption for vessels does not apply, and he must pay for the clothes.

keyTerms.meaning: And רב? (meaning: how would רב answer this?)

steps.whatToRemember: For רב, the בור exemption for vessels applies only to objects that were made הפקר. If the owner still owns the object, he pays for vessels too.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the real argument: is an object lying in the street always treated like a בור, or only once its owner has given it up?

phrases.english: And Rav?
phrases.notes: The גמרא is asking how רב would answer שמואל's argument.

phrases.english: These words apply where he made them ownerless,
phrases.notes: 'These words' are the idea that a stone, knife or load is learned from a pit.

phrases.english: but where he did not make them ownerless —
it is his property.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב – הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּאַפְקְרִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רב against שמואל's argument by limiting when the comparison to בור applies.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the source (only ownerless objects are like בור)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every object left in the street is like a בור, so the owner is always exempt for vessels.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only an object made הפקר is like a בור. An object still owned counts as the owner's property, so he pays for vessels such as the clothes.

steps.title: רב אושעיא brings a teaching about the pit
steps.stepSummary: רב אושעיא quotes a ברייתא. It says בור is liable for animals but exempt for people and vessels, and that objects left in the street are similar to בור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אושעיא objects: the פסוק says 'an ox or a donkey falls there.' An ox, but not a person. A donkey, but not vessels. So if an ox or donkey falls into a pit together with its equipment, the digger pays for the animal but not for the equipment. And objects left in the street are compared to this.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אושעיא starts an objection by quoting a ברייתא. This step only sets up the source. The actual difficulty comes in step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learns from the פסוק that בור never pays for vessels. It then links stones, knives, and loads left in רשות הרבים to בור. That link is what will cause trouble for רב, who said such objects pay even for vessels unless the owner made them הפקר.

keyTerms.meaning: a pit, one of the main categories of damage

phrases.english: Rav Oshaya raises an objection:
"And an ox or a donkey fall there";
"Ox", but not "person";
"Donkey", but not vessels.
From here they said:
If an ox and its equipment fell into it and they broke,
or a donkey and its equipment, and they tore,
he is liable for the animal,
and exempt for the equipment.
To what is this similar?
To his stone, his knife, or his load
that he left in the public domain, and they caused damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתִיב רַב אוֹשַׁעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new source to test רב's view as explained in step 4, and שמואל's view from step 3.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא puts objects in the street in the same group as בור, which is exempt for vessels. Step 9 will spell out the full difficulty.

steps.title: The comparison is worded backwards
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the ברייתא should have said 'what is similar to this,' because the objects are learned from בור, not the other way around.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary, it should have said 'What is similar to this?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to question the wording of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא asked what בור is similar to, and answered with the stone, knife, and load. But בור is written in the תורה, and the objects are learned from it. So the question should start from בור and ask what is similar to it.

phrases.english: On the contrary, it should have said "What is similar to this?"
phrases.notes: בור is the main case in the פסוק, so the stone and knife should be compared to it, not the reverse.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּרַבָּה, מָה דּוֹמֶה לָזֶה מִבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the last line of the ברייתא quoted in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording 'הא למה זה דומה' in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The source case is בור, so the sentence should ask what is like בור, not what בור is like.

steps.title: Fixing the wording of the comparison
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rewords the ברייתא: 'What is similar to this? A stone, knife, or load left in the street.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, read it like this: What is similar to this? His stone, his knife, or his load that he left in the public domain, and they caused damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the wording so that the objects are compared to בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing changes in the law. The order is simply corrected, so that בור is the source and the objects in the street are learned from it.

phrases.english: Rather: What is similar to this?
His stone, his knife, or his load
that he left in the public domain, and they caused damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מַאי דּוֹמֶה לָזֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question of step 6.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to learn בור from the objects in the street.
steps.terutzMaskana: The objects in the street are learned from בור.

steps.title: A flask broken on a stone
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends: if someone breaks his flask on a stone left in the street, the stone's owner is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore, if he smashed his flask on a stone, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to quoting the ברייתא, which gives one more ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the damaged item is a vessel, a flask, and the stone's owner still pays. That seems to clash with the earlier part of the ברייתא, which said בור does not pay for vessels.

phrases.english: Therefore,
if he smashed his flask on a stone, he is liable.
phrases.notes: He means the owner of the stone has to pay for the broken flask.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְפִיכָךְ, אִם הֵטִיחַ צְלוֹחִיתוֹ בְּאֶבֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from step 5 after the wording fix of steps 6 and 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner of a stone in the street pays for a vessel broken on it.

steps.title: The beginning troubles רב, and the end troubles שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא states the double difficulty. The first part of the ברייתא goes against רב, and the last part goes against שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: The first part is difficult for רב, and the last part is difficult for שמואל!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now says plainly what the problem with the ברייתא is. It makes trouble for both אמוראים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part compares objects in the street to בור without saying anything about הפקר. That means they would be exempt for vessels even when not made הפקר, against רב. The last part makes the stone's owner pay for a flask, which is a vessel, against שמואל, who said objects in the street are exempt for vessels.

keyTerms.meaning: the first part of a teaching
the last part of a teaching

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא seems to contradict itself. בור is exempt for vessels, yet the stone's owner pays for the flask. So רב is troubled by the beginning and שמואל by the end.
steps.confusionAlert: The problem with the ברייתא is not about bodily injury at all. Both parts of the difficulty are about whether the owner pays for vessels.

phrases.english: The first part is difficult for Rav,
and the last part is difficult for Shmuel!

steps.triggerLanguage: רֵישָׁא קַשְׁיָא לְרַב, וְסֵיפָא קַשְׁיָא לִשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the difficulty that רב אושעיא's objection in step 5 was building toward, using both parts of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's view in step 4 and שמואל's view in step 3
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first part makes objects in the street fully like בור, with no mention of הפקר, against רב. The last part makes the owner pay for a vessel, against שמואל's exemption for vessels.

steps.title: The ברייתא contradicts itself anyway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: the ברייתא's first and last parts seem to clash with each other, so it is not a special problem for רב or שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And by your own logic, the ברייתא itself should bother you: the first part says the owner is exempt, and the last part says he is liable!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the double challenge by showing that the ברייתא already seems to contradict itself, no matter whose view you hold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רישא says objects in the street are like בור, so the owner is exempt for broken vessels. The סיפא says the owner of a stone is liable for a broken flask. Since the ברייתא must be explained anyway, each אמורא can explain it his own way, so the challenge loses its force.

keyTerms.meaning: And according to your own reasoning; a way of turning the question back on the one asking
It itself; the source contradicts itself
The first part of a teaching
The last part of a teaching

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the ברייתא is wrong. It is saying the ברייתא needs explaining for everyone, so it cannot be used to knock down רב or שמואל.

phrases.english: And according to your reasoning,
the ברייתא itself should be difficult for you:
(it is difficult:) the first part says exempt,
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets. The meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: and the last part says liable!
phrases.notes: This is the broken flask case from step 8.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְטַעְמָיךְ, תִּיקְשֵׁי לָךְ הִיא גּוּפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes back against the double challenge of step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the ברייתא can be used as proof against רב or שמואל.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא seems self-contradictory, so it must be explained no matter whose view you hold.

steps.title: Each one explains the ברייתא his own way
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא announces that רב and שמואל will each explain the ברייתא according to his own view.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב explains it according to his view, and שמואל explains it according to his view.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is preparing to show how each אמורא explains the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the ברייתא needs explaining anyway, each side can explain it in a way that fits his own view. The next two steps give the details.

keyTerms.meaning: Explains it according to his own reasoning

phrases.english: Rather, רב explains it according to his reasoning,
and שמואל explains it according to his reasoning.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא רַב מְתָרֵץ לְטַעְמֵיהּ, וּשְׁמוּאֵל מְתָרֵץ לְטַעְמֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 10: since the ברייתא needs explaining anyway, each side explains it his way.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Framework announcement: each side reads the ברייתא in his own way
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא disproves both רב and שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each one can read the ברייתא so it fits his view.

steps.title: רב's explanation: the first part is about objects the owner gave up
steps.stepSummary: רב says the exemption in the first part applies only when the owner gave up ownership (הפקר). If he still owns the objects, he is liable, and that is why the owner of the stone pays for the flask.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב explains it his way: When is this said? When he gave up ownership of them. But if he did not give up ownership, he is liable. So if someone broke his flask on a stone, the owner is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רב limits the first part of the ברייתא to objects that were made הפקר. That way, the last part (about a stone someone still owns) fits his view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, only an object the owner gave up counts like a בור, where he is exempt for broken vessels. An object he still owns makes him liable even for vessels. So the רישא is about הפקר objects, and the סיפא is about objects still owned.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case is this said? A way of narrowing a rule to a specific case
He gave up ownership of them (made them ownerless)

phrases.english: רב explains it according to his reasoning:
In what case is this said?
When he gave up ownership of them,
phrases.notes: This is the first part of the ברייתא, where stone, knife and load are like a בור and the owner is exempt for vessels.

phrases.english: but if he did not give up ownership of them, he is liable.
Therefore, if one broke his flask on a stone, the owner is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב מְתָרֵץ לְטַעְמֵיהּ, בַּמֶּה דְּבָרִים אֲמוּרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first of the two explanations announced in step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the רישא is limited to הפקר objects
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רישא exempts the owner for vessels in every case, which goes against רב.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רישא is only about הפקר objects. Owned objects make the owner liable, as the סיפא says.

steps.title: שמואל's explanation: the last part follows רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: שמואל keeps the rule that a stone, knife and load are like a בור. He explains that the last part follows רבי יהודה, who makes a בור owner pay for broken vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל explains it his way: Now that you said his stone, knife and load are like his בור, then according to רבי יהודה, who makes a person liable for vessels damaged in a בור, therefore if someone broke his flask on a stone, the owner is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל agrees the objects are like a בור. He says the last part of the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה's view about vessels in a בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שמואל, these objects are always like a בור, even if the owner still owns them. Most hold a בור owner is exempt for vessels, which is the רישא. But רבי יהודה makes him pay for vessels, and the סיפא follows רבי יהודה, so the owner pays for the flask.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: objects in the street are like a בור only when made הפקר. If owned, the owner pays even for vessels. שמואל: they are always like a בור, and the flask case follows רבי יהודה, who makes a בור owner pay for vessels.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a common גמרא method: each side keeps his own view by explaining a hard source differently. One limits the case, and the other ties part of the source to a specific תנא.

phrases.english: And שמואל explains it according to his reasoning:
Now that you said
his stone, his knife and his load are like his pit,
then according to רבי יהודה, who holds one liable
for damage to vessels in a pit,
therefore, if one broke his flask on a stone, the owner is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל מְתָרֵץ לְטַעְמֵיהּ, הַשְׁתָּא דְּאָמְרַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second explanation announced in step 11, alongside רב's in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Linking the סיפא to a specific תנא (רבי יהודה)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The סיפא makes the owner of the stone liable for vessels, which goes against שמואל's view that it is like a בור.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is still like a בור, but the סיפא follows רבי יהודה, who makes a בור owner pay for vessels.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר limits the stone owner's liability
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says the stone owner pays only when the person tripped on the stone and the flask broke on the stone. If he tripped on the ground and the flask broke on the stone, the owner is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: The ruling that the stone owner pays applies only when the walker tripped on the stone and the flask scraped against the stone. But if he tripped on the ground and the flask scraped against the stone, the owner is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר narrows the ברייתא's last part, which said the owner of the stone pays for a broken flask.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He separates two causes: what made the person fall, and what broke the flask. The stone owner pays only if his stone did both. If the ground caused the fall, the stone only finished the damage, so its owner is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this when, a formula that limits a ruling to one case
Scraped against (the flask hit the stone and broke)

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
They taught it only where he tripped on the stone,
phrases.notes: He is talking about the ברייתא's last part, where the stone owner pays for the flask.

phrases.english: and it scraped against the stone.
But if he tripped on the ground
and it scraped against the stone, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the case in the ברייתא's last part that רב and שמואל just explained.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The stone owner is liable only if the stone caused both the fall and the breaking.

steps.title: Whose view is this? Not רבי נתן's
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whose opinion the first version follows and answers that it does not follow רבי נתן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is this? It is not the view of רבי נתן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which תנא the first version fits, and answers that it goes against רבי נתן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי נתן holds that when two things cause damage together and one of them cannot be made to pay, the other pays the full amount. By that rule, the stone owner should pay even when the ground caused the fall. Since רבי אלעזר exempts him, this version disagrees with רבי נתן.

phrases.english: In accordance with whom?
Not in accordance with Rabbi Natan.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies which תנא the first version of רבי אלעזר follows.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא's view the first version of רבי אלעזר follows.

steps.title: The second version: liable even if he tripped on the ground
steps.stepSummary: In another version, רבי אלעזר says the stone owner is liable even when the person tripped on the ground and the flask broke on the stone.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רבי אלעזר said: Do not think he is liable only when he tripped on the stone and the flask scraped against the stone, but exempt when he tripped on the ground and the flask scraped against the stone. Rather, even if he tripped on the ground and the flask scraped against the stone, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of רבי אלעזר's statement, which reaches the opposite result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the stone only needs to be what broke the flask. What made the person fall does not matter. So instead of limiting the owner's liability, this version widens it.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not say (do not think that)

steps.confusionAlert: Both versions come from the same רבי אלעזר. They are two reports of what he said, not two different rabbis arguing.

phrases.english: Some say: Rabbi Elazar said:
Do not say that when he tripped on the stone
and it scraped against the stone, that is when he is liable,
but if he tripped on the ground
and it scraped against the stone, he is exempt;
rather, even if he tripped on the ground
and it scraped against the stone, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: לָא תֵּימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of step 14 that reverses its result.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The stone owner is liable whenever the flask breaks on his stone, even if the person tripped on the ground.

steps.title: The second version follows רבי נתן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whose view the second version follows and answers that it follows רבי נתן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is this? It is the view of רבי נתן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא identifies the second version as following רבי נתן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ground cannot be made to pay, so by רבי נתן's rule the stone owner pays the full damage. This version therefore fits רבי נתן, while the first version went against him.
steps.whatToRemember: The two versions of רבי אלעזר depend on רבי נתן's rule. The first version (exempt) goes against רבי נתן, and the second version (liable) follows him.

phrases.english: In accordance with whom? In accordance with Rabbi Natan.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַאן – כְּרַבִּי נָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallels step 15 and places the second version on רבי נתן's side.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא's view the second version follows.

steps.title: What does רבי יהודה mean by 'with intent'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה, where רבי יהודה says the owner of a broken jug is liable if he acted with intent, and asks what counts as intent.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: If he acted with intent, he is liable, and so on. What is the case of 'with intent'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line in the משנה and asks what 'with intent' means. This sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, someone's jug broke in the public domain, and רבי יהודה makes the owner liable only if he acted with intent. The word is unclear, because nobody normally means to break his own jug. So the גמרא asks for the exact case.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? (What are the circumstances?)
And so on, a sign that the quote from the משנה continues

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
phrases.notes: This is quoted from our משנה about a jug that broke in the public domain.

phrases.english: If he acted with intent, he is liable, and so on.
What is the case of 'with intent'?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי מִתְכַּוֵּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of רבי אלעזר and returns to the משנה to explain רבי יהודה's view.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What case of 'acting with intent' רבי יהודה has in mind.

steps.title: רבה defines intent as even intending to lower the jug
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that the 'intent' רבי יהודה requires is only that the person meant to lower the jug off his shoulder.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה says: It means where he intended to lower the jug down from his shoulder.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers the question from the last step about what 'intent' means in רבי יהודה's view. Even just meaning to take the jug down from his shoulder counts as intent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The intent is not about breaking the jug or blocking the road. If he chose to lower the jug and it broke while he did so, רבי יהודה already holds him liable. Only if the jug broke with no action of his own is he exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: to lower it, to take it down

phrases.english: Rabba says:
Where he intends to lower it
phrases.notes: 'It' is the jug from the משנה.

phrases.english: down from his shoulder.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: בְּמִתְכַּוֵּין לְהוֹרִידָהּ לְמַטָּה מִכְּתֵיפוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18 about what counts as 'intent'.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Intent means only that he intended to lower the jug from his shoulder, even though he did not intend to break it.

steps.title: אביי infers how far רבי מאיר's liability goes
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks whether, by implication, רבי מאיר holds the person liable even when the jug fell apart on its own.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Does that mean that רבי מאיר holds him liable even if the jug cracked by itself?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי draws a conclusion from רבה's answer and checks whether רבה really means it. If רבי יהודה needs only this small amount of intent to make him liable, then רבי מאיר, who disagrees, must hold him liable even with no intent at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה and רבי מאיר argue in the משנה. רבה made רבי יהודה's liability very broad, so the only cases left for רבי מאיר to differ on are ones with no action at all. אביי asks whether רבה accepts that this leads to liability even when the jug falls apart on its own.

keyTerms.meaning: by implication, from this it follows
it fell apart or cracked by itself

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה is the one who exempts unless there was intent. רבי מאיר is the stricter opinion that holds him liable even without intent.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
Does it follow that Rabbi Meir holds him liable
phrases.notes: רבי מאיר is the first, unnamed opinion in the משנה, the one who argues with רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: even if it cracked by itself?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: מִכְּלָל דִּמְחַיֵּיב רַבִּי מֵאִיר אֲפִילּוּ נִפְשְׁרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from רבה's definition of intent and applies it to רבי מאיר.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבה's definition forces the conclusion that רבי מאיר holds a person liable even when the jug breaks with no act of his.

steps.title: רבה agrees that רבי מאיר holds him liable even holding the handle
steps.stepSummary: רבה agrees: רבי מאיר holds him liable even if he was holding the jug properly by its handle.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to him: Yes. רבי מאיר would hold him liable even if he was holding the jug's handle in his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה accepts אביי's inference and goes even further. In רבי מאיר's view, the person is liable even in the most careful situation, holding the jug by its handle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding the handle is the right way to carry a jug, so if it breaks anyway, that is pure bad luck. רבה says רבי מאיר still holds him liable. This sets up the strong challenge in the next step.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes,
Rabbi Meir would hold him liable
even if its handle was in his hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִין, מְחַיֵּיב הָיָה רַבִּי מֵאִיר אֲפִילּוּ אׇזְנָהּ בְּיָדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question with a yes and extends it.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. רבי מאיר holds him liable even when he held the jug by its handle, which is a complete accident.

steps.title: Challenge: the תורה exempts someone who is forced
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why he should be liable at all, since he is אנוס and the תורה exempts an אנוס, as learned from the נערה המאורסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? He is forced by circumstances beyond his control, and the Merciful One exempts someone who is forced, as it is written: 'But to the young woman you shall do nothing.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבה's explanation of רבי מאיר. A person who truly could not help it is called אנוס, and the תורה does not hold an אנוס responsible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source is the betrothed girl who was forced. The תורה says not to punish her because she had no choice. That shows a general rule that אונס exempts, so how can רבי מאיר hold someone liable when the handle broke in his hand?

keyTerms.meaning: someone forced, with no control over what happened

phrases.english: Why? He is forced by circumstances!
And the Merciful One exempts one who is forced,
as it is written:
"But to the young woman you shall do nothing!"

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמַּאי? אָנוּס הוּא, וְאוֹנֶס רַחֲמָנָא פַּטְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's claim that רבי מאיר holds a person liable even for a complete accident.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's statement that רבי מאיר holds him liable even if the handle was in his hand
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The תורה exempts an אנוס, as the פסוק about the נערה shows. Holding a person liable for a pure accident contradicts that rule.

steps.title: A possible answer: the exemption applies only to the death penalty
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a possible defense: the אונס exemption may apply only to capital punishment, not to paying for damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say that this applies only to the death penalty, but for damages he is liable,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a possible answer to its own challenge. This step sets up the next move, where the גמרא will knock this answer down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about the נערה deals with the death penalty. Perhaps the exemption of אונס is limited to that, while paying for damage is owed even by an אנוס. This would rescue רבה's reading of רבי מאיר.

keyTerms.meaning: and if you would say (introduces a possible answer that will be rejected)

phrases.english: And if you would say these words apply
only regarding the death penalty,
but regarding damages, he is liable;

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא הָנֵי מִילֵּי לְעִנְיַן קְטָלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a possible defense against the challenge of step 22, which the גמרא is about to reject.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of a rule (the אונס exemption applies only to capital punishment)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אונס exempts in every area of law, including damages.
steps.terutzMaskana: Perhaps אונס exempts only from the death penalty, so a person still pays for damages.

steps.title: A ברייתא about a broken jug and a fallen camel
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggested defense by bringing a ברייתא where רבי מאיר and חכמים argue about a jug that broke and a camel that fell.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't it taught in a ברייתא: If his jug broke and he did not remove it, or his camel fell and he did not stand it up, רבי מאיר holds him liable for the damage they cause, and חכמים say:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show that the answer in the last step does not work. The ברייתא, and the rest of the argument, continue on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is about damages, not the death penalty. It will show that even regarding damages, אונס is treated as an exemption. Note that רבי מאיר holds him liable here because he did not clean up afterward, not for the breaking itself.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught in a ברייתא:
His jug broke and he did not remove it,
phrases.notes: He did not clear away the broken pieces.

phrases.english: his camel fell and he did not stand it up —
Rabbi Meir holds him liable for the damage they cause,
and the Rabbis say:

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: נִשְׁבְּרָה כַּדּוֹ וְלֹא סִלְּקָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the possible defense of step 23 using a ברייתא about damages.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that the אונס exemption applies only to the death penalty
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא dealing with damages, a broken jug and a fallen camel, will show that אונס matters even for damages. So the limitation to the death penalty fails.
